reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is a news-style consumer warning about a text message claiming a $1,000 Walmart gift-card promotion. The presenter describes receiving the message, advises viewers to check suspicious texts, and instructs them to Google the message rather than click its link. The segment presents the link as potentially harmful and does not show the creator promoting it.

citations.quote: your code printed on your last receipt is among seven we randomly picked for a $1,000 Walmart gift card promotion
So instead of clicking that link right there, I Googled it first.
Do this with any strange text or call you ever get.
In this case it turned out to be an old scam from 2012.
clicking on that link could infect your phone with the virus or take you to a site where they try to get your personal information to steal your identity

opening.argument: Judge the promise and the action together. The displayed message tells a named recipient that a receipt code was selected for a $1,000 gift card, then presents a link alongside that claim. The speaker explicitly connects the link to the offer when explaining what he chose not to click. That is a concrete reward-to-link pathway, not merely a discussion of gift cards in the abstract. The warning does not remove the solicitation contained in the message viewers are shown.

citations.quote: congrats Ben, your code printed on your last receipt is among seven we randomly picked for a $1,000 Walmart gift card promotion.
So instead of clicking that link right there, I Googled it first.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense is right that the presenter says he searched instead of clicking. That establishes his response, but it does not erase the offer and link displayed to viewers. Nor does calling the message an old scam change the mechanism under review: a purported free reward is tied to a link that the speaker identifies as dangerous.

citations.quote: In this case it turned out to be an old scam from 2012.
clicking on that link could infect your phone with the virus or take you to a site where they try to get your personal information to steal your identity

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The reward-to-link pathway belongs to the suspicious text being examined, not to an offer made by the presenter. He tells viewers he did not click, instructs them to check strange messages, and identifies this one as an old scam. Showing the message as evidence of a threat is not soliciting viewers to claim its reward.

citations.quote: So instead of clicking that link right there, I Googled it first.
Do this with any strange text or call you ever get.
In this case it turned out to be an old scam from 2012.

opening.argument: The suspicious message combines several concrete signals: an unsolicited text, a personalized claim that a receipt code was among seven selected, a $1,000 reward, and a link. The presenter also describes what following that link could lead to: phone infection or a site seeking personal information. Taken together, these details support treating the displayed offer as a deceptive attempt to draw a recipient into a reward-claim flow. The real possibility of Walmart gift cards through surveys does not validate this text-based winner claim.

citations.quote: I got this text out of the blue saying, congrats Ben, your code printed on your last receipt is among seven we randomly picked for a $1,000 Walmart gift card promotion.
clicking on that link could infect your phone with the virus or take you to a site where they try to get your personal information to steal your identity
but they would never text you to say you won. They would send it in a certified letter.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense emphasizes the warning, but its own quoted account identifies the risky mechanism: the text announces a reward and supplies a link whose destination may seek personal information. The instruction to Google first addresses how to avoid the attempt; it does not make the attempt any less deceptive.

citations.quote: So instead of clicking that link right there, I Googled it first.
clicking on that link could infect your phone with the virus or take you to a site where they try to get your personal information to steal your identity

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Those signals establish why the third-party text is suspicious, not why the video should be treated as a solicitation. The speaker describes the message as an old scam and directs viewers to search before acting. His account of possible harm is a reason to avoid the link, not an invitation to use it.

citations.quote: In this case it turned out to be an old scam from 2012.
So instead of clicking that link right there, I Googled it first.
So remember, anytime something looks too good to be true. Google it first.

opening.argument: A warning format can still put a claim-and-link combination directly before an audience. Here the message is displayed prominently while the presenter recounts its $1,000 gift-card promise; later, he acknowledges that Walmart does give away gift cards through online surveys. That legitimate-sounding comparison may make the reward premise seem plausible even as he disputes this particular text. The judge should consider the practical exposure created by displaying the offer and its link, not rely solely on the presenter's stated intent.

citations.quote: your code printed on your last receipt is among seven we randomly picked for a $1,000 Walmart gift card promotion
The CBS station in Denver did do an old story about how Walmart does give away $1000 gift cards for completing surveys online

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense points to advice to Google the text and to warnings about the link. Those are real, but they answer what the presenter says, not the effect of repeatedly displaying the reward message and its link. The survey comparison also leaves a viewer with confirmation that some Walmart gift-card giveaways exist, while the crucial distinction is how winners are contacted.

citations.quote: The CBS station in Denver did do an old story about how Walmart does give away $1000 gift cards for completing surveys online
but they would never text you to say you won. They would send it in a certified letter.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Visibility alone does not turn a warning into promotion. The speaker supplies the decisive distinction immediately after mentioning real surveys: Walmart would not notify a winner by text. He says he avoided the link, identifies the message as an old scam, and warns that clicking could compromise a phone or personal information. The opening identifies exposure to a scam example, not encouragement to participate.
